messages.subject: Occupancy data for diversity indices
parts:
Hello all,

There's been some discussion about using Unmarked for estimating species richness, but I wanted to bounce an alternative approach off the group.  I'd like to use occupancy data to calculate Shannon-Weiner diversity indices (i.e., accounting for species evenness in addition to richness). The idea would be to:
1) use pcount to estimate local abundance of each species at each sampling site
2) use those estimates to calculate predicted diversity at each site
3) determine which covariates are related to variation in diversity among sites.

My question is this: at what point should the covariates be entered into the analysis?  I can see two potential strategies:

A) The covariates are entered at step 1 by being incorporated into the abundance function in pcount. But then when data from multiple species are "pooled" into the diversity index, how would I assess the effects of each covariate on overall diversity?  One option would be to just look at the R-squared value of simple relationships between diversity and each covariate individually. 

B) I could use ranef() in step 1 to generate site-specific abundance estimates for each species without accounting for any covariates, then calculate site-specific diversity, then run regression models to see how overall diversity is related to the covariates, individually and jointly. 

What would people think of the validity of either of these approaches, or are there any better suggestions out there?

Many thanks in advance.

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Occupancy data for diversity indices
parts:
Hi Jedediah,

I think it would be very difficult to properly account for uncertainty using the methods you suggest. I recommend looking at the models described by Dorazio and Royle (JASA 2005), Dorazio et al. (Ecology 2006), Royle and Dorazio (2008 Ch12). Elise Zipkin and others have some good papers in which they apply the model. Yuichi Yamaura and colleagues have a couple of papers in which they extend the model for count data.

I wanted to add this model to unmarked, but even in the simplest case, with no covariates, the likelihood evaluations were too slow to be of much use. So I would use JAGS.

Richard
